questions.question_text: A car used $36$ L of petrol to travel $450$ km. What is its fuel consumption rate in L/100 km?

options.why: Divided the distance by the fuel, which gives the rate in km/L, then labelled it as L/100 km.
Divided the litres by the kilometres but did not scale the answer up to $100$ km.
Multiplied the litres by the distance instead of dividing, then divided by $100$.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{36\text{ L}}{450\text{ km}} = \dfrac{x\text{ L}}{100\text{ km}}$
$x = \dfrac{36}{450} \times 100$
$= 8\text{ L/100 km}$

questions.question_text: A car's fuel consumption rate is $25$ km/L. What is this rate in L/100 km?

options.why: Multiplied the rate by $100$ instead of dividing $100$ by the rate.
Found the litres used per kilometre and did not scale it up to $100$ km.
Divided $1000$ by the rate instead of $100$, as if the rate were per $1000$ km.

questions.question_text: A four-wheel drive uses fuel at $12.6$ L/100 km. How much fuel does it use on a trip of $275$ km?

options.why: Multiplied the rate by the distance but forgot that the rate is per $100$ km.
Divided the distance by the rate as if the rate were litres per kilometre.
Used the method for finding a distance, dividing by the rate and then multiplying by $100$.

questions.question_text: A car uses fuel at $7.2$ L/100 km. How far can it travel on $45$ L of petrol?

options.why: Divided the litres by the rate but did not scale the answer up by the $100$ km.
Multiplied the litres by the rate instead of dividing.
Used the method for finding fuel used, multiplying by the rate and dividing by $100$.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{7.2\text{ L}}{100\text{ km}} = \dfrac{45\text{ L}}{x\text{ km}}$
$\dfrac{100\text{ km}}{7.2\text{ L}} = \dfrac{x\text{ km}}{45\text{ L}}$
$x = \dfrac{100}{7.2} \times 45$
$= 625\text{ km}$

questions.question_text: A car uses fuel at $10.4$ L/100 km and is driven $640$ km. Petrol costs $\$1.75$ per litre. What is the fuel cost for the trip?

options.why: Multiplied the distance by the price per litre without using the consumption rate to find the litres.
Forgot to divide by $100$ when finding the litres, using $6656$ L instead of $66.56$ L.
Divided the litres by the price per litre instead of multiplying.

questions.question_text: Car J uses fuel at $6.5$ L/100 km. Car K travels $16$ km on each litre of fuel. Comparing litres used per $100$ km, which car is more efficient and by how much?

options.why: Treated the two rates as directly proportional and compared $16$ with $6.5$ directly, so the smaller number looked more efficient.
Chose the right car but subtracted the two given numbers instead of converting the km/L rate to L/100 km first.

options.text: The two cars are equally efficient
options.why: Assumed $16$ km/L and $6.5$ L/100 km must describe the same efficiency because both rates involve $100$ km.

questions.solution_text:
Car K: $\dfrac{100}{16}$
$= 6.25\text{ L/100 km}$
Car J: $6.5\text{ L/100 km}$
$6.5 - 6.25$
$= 0.25\text{ L/100 km}$
Car K uses less fuel per $100$ km, so Car K is more efficient by $0.25$ L/100 km.

questions.question_text: A car uses fuel at $7.4$ L/100 km on the highway and $10.5$ L/100 km in the city. It makes a trip of $520$ km that includes $60$ km of city driving. How much fuel does the trip use?

options.why: Applied the highway rate to the full $520$ km instead of subtracting the $60$ km of city driving first.
Swapped the rates, using the city rate for the highway kilometres and the highway rate for the city kilometres.
Averaged the two rates and applied that single rate to the whole $520$ km.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{highway} = 520 - 60$
$= 460\text{ km}$
Highway fuel: $7.4 \times \dfrac{460}{100}$
$= 34.04\text{ L}$
City fuel: $10.5 \times \dfrac{60}{100}$
$= 6.3\text{ L}$
$34.04 + 6.3$
$= 40.34\text{ L}$

questions.question_text: A motorcycle travelled $464$ km on $16$ L of fuel. What is its fuel consumption rate in km/L?

options.why: Calculated the rate in L/100 km and labelled the answer as km/L.
Divided the litres by the kilometres, putting the two quantities the wrong way round.
Multiplied the distance by the litres instead of dividing.
